posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-value CRO post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the auditability pain from a compliance-first angle, position explainability as the real unlock without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' problem is exactly why auditability has become the thing finance teams care about more than speed or accuracy. A number that's right but can't be traced is almost as dangerous as a number that's wrong — maybe more, because it looks trustworthy. Curious whether the ban was the end of it for your team, or whether you're still looking for something that can actually close that gap.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person consultancy frustrated with Power BI adoption — validate the trust problem specifically, add the insight that this is a data credibility issue not a tool issue
posts.draft_comment: The trust gap is almost always the actual problem. People don't refuse dashboards because they're lazy — they refuse them because they've been burned once by a number that was wrong, or defined differently than they expected, and now Excel feels safer because at least they built it themselves. 18 months of dashboard work can collapse the moment someone spots one figure that doesn't match their spreadsheet. What does your finance team say when you ask them what it would actually take to trust it?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard bloat — validate the 10%-to-85% usage flip with a sharper insight about why fewer metrics actually builds trust, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 to 5 is the move almost nobody has the nerve to make. The counterintuitive thing I keep seeing is that fewer metrics doesn't mean less visibility — it means people actually trust what they're looking at. When everything is measured, nothing is accountable. Who pushed back hardest when you cut the list?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on self-service BI chaos — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the insight that the tooling problem is actually a trust problem in disguise
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so recognisable. Everyone's technically empowered and yet somehow nobody trusts any number that didn't come from Dave in Finance. I think the self-service dream quietly assumed everyone would converge on shared definitions — but tools don't create that, culture does. Who actually owns the truth in your org right now, Mark — is it a person, a team, or is it still up for debate?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO raising AI hallucinations as a material risk with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the security framing, add the specific mechanic that makes analytics hallucinations uniquely dangerous
posts.draft_comment: The financial report example is the one that keeps people up at night. What makes analytics hallucinations worse than most AI errors is that the output *looks* like it came from your data — it has the right columns, the right formatting, the right vibe. So it bypasses the scepticism you'd apply to something that obviously looked wrong. At what point does 'the AI said so' become enough audit trail for a CFO to sign off?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: COO at a Sterling Consulting (ICP prospect) engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical teams — validate the core pain with a specific observation, add a sharper diagnosis
posts.draft_comment: The £200k number hurts but the real cost is the 49 people who just stopped asking questions. That's what never shows up in the ROI deck. Most tools were designed to impress in a demo, not survive contact with someone who just wants to know why margin dropped last month. Wonder how many renewals happen simply because no one wants to admit it didn't work?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a likely mid-market industrial company hits a universal BI credibility problem — validate the real root cause (governance, not AI) and add a layer he hasn't named yet
posts.draft_comment: The filter thing is almost never the real problem — it's that nobody agreed on what the number was *supposed* to mean before anyone built the dashboard. Three teams, three definitions, all technically correct. Culture helps, but I'd argue the fight starts earlier than that: who owns the definition, not just the data. Has your CFO started questioning the other numbers now too?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing real adoption failure with enterprise AI — validate the 'nobody knows what to ask' insight with a sharper diagnosis about data literacy, not tool lockdown
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is brutal but honestly pretty typical. The shadow AI thing is interesting though — people aren't going to ChatGPT because it's less locked down, they're going because it feels like a conversation rather than a command prompt. The real gap isn't access, it's that most people don't have a mental model of what questions their data can even answer. Copilot sitting on top of that problem doesn't fix it, it just makes the problem shinier.
